name: unzip2
summary: Splits a list of two-field rows into two parallel columns, returned as two values.
explanation: zip weaves parallel lists into rows; unzip2 unweaves rows back into two parallel lists. It is the exact inverse, and it is where the multiple-value return earns its keep -- returning a two-element list of columns would force every caller to car and cadr the result apart, which is the same unwrapping the verb was called to perform. Instead it hands back two values, and define-values or call-with-values binds them to two names in one line. That matters because the whole point of unzipping is to get two things you can work with independently: xs and ys to plot, keys and values to build a table, inputs and expectations to run a test suite. The verb reads exactly two fields from each row and requires both to be there. A row of one is not a row with a blank second column; it is malformed, and it raises.

examples.code:
(define-values (nums letters) (unzip2 '((1 a) (2 b) (3 c))))
(display (list nums letters))
(newline)
examples.note: ((1 2 3) (a b c)) -- one call, two columns, bound to two names.
(names (ann bo) ages (31 24) oldest 31) -- call-with-values is the form to use when the columns are consumed on the spot.

examples.code:
(define pairs '((1 10) (2 20) (3 30)))
(define-values (ks vs) (unzip2 pairs))
(define rebuilt (map (lambda (k v) (list k v)) ks vs))
(display (list 'keys ks 'vals vs 'round-trip (equal? rebuilt pairs)))
(newline)
examples.note: (keys (1 2 3) vals (10 20 30) round-trip #t) -- unzipping and re-zipping returns the table unchanged.

caveats: It returns TWO VALUES, not a list of two lists. Calling (car (unzip2 rows)) does not work -- use define-values or call-with-values.
Every row must have at least two elements. A one-element row raises rather than leaving a hole.
Rows longer than two are accepted and the extra fields are dropped silently. Use unzip3 if you meant to keep the third.
On an empty list of rows it answers two empty lists, which is the right identity for re-zipping.
The columns are fresh lists; the elements inside them are shared with the original rows.
It is defined on lists-of-lists, not on lists of dotted pairs. For an association list of (key . value) cells, map car and map cdr are the right calls.
usecases: Splitting a list of (x y) points into separate coordinate lists for plotting or statistics.
Turning a list of (input expected) test cases into two parallel lists for a runner.
Recovering the two columns that zip wove together, so each can be transformed independently.

learn.concept: When a verb naturally produces two answers, returning two values is honest -- packing them in a list just makes the caller unpack it.
learn.progression: Zip two lists into rows and look at the result. Then try to get them back with map car and map cadr -- two traversals and two chances to mismatch. Then use unzip2 and bind both at once, and notice that define-values exists precisely for verbs shaped like this.

row-2-audit.math-program:
(define (centroid points)
  (call-with-values (lambda () (unzip2 points))
    (lambda (xs ys)
      (list (/ (apply + xs) (length xs)) (/ (apply + ys) (length ys))))))
(display (map centroid '(((0 0) (2 0) (1 3)) ((4 4)) ((0 0) (0 8) (8 0) (8 8)))))
(newline)
row-2-audit.cs-program:
(define (columns rows)
  (call-with-values (lambda () (unzip2 rows)) (lambda (a b) (list (length a) (length b) a b))))
(display (list 'square (columns '((1 2) (3 4)))
               'wide (columns '((1 2 99) (3 4 98)))
               'empty (columns '())))
(newline)
row-2-audit.problem: A test runner receives a list of (input expected) cases and needs to feed the inputs to a function while holding the expectations for comparison. Candidates: unzip2 (one traversal, both columns, and the multiple-value return means the two names are bound together so they cannot drift apart), (list (map car cases) (map cadr cases)) (two traversals, and the result is a list the caller has to take apart again), mapping over the rows and destructuring each one inline (fine when the two fields are used together, but here they are used at different times -- the inputs run first, the expectations compare later), zip (the wrong direction entirely -- these are already rows), a fold building two accumulators (correct and five lines, and it is what unzip2 already is). unzip2 is the pick because the two columns have different lifetimes.
row-2-audit.explanation: eng: splitting test cases into inputs and expectations for three case lists, including a single case and none at all. math: a centroid, which needs both coordinate columns reduced independently and then recombined, over a triangle, a single point, and a square. cs: reporting both column lengths alongside the columns, on a square table, a wider one where the third field is dropped, and an empty one -- which shows the two columns are always the same length as each other and as the input.
row-2-audit.meta: The wide case in the cs program is deliberate. unzip2 accepting a three-field row and silently discarding the third is a real hazard, and the only defence is knowing it happens.
row-2-audit.eng: Two columns bound by one form cannot get out of step. Two separate map calls can, the moment someone edits one of them.
row-2-audit.math: A centroid is the componentwise mean, and componentwise operations on points want the components separated. Unzipping first is what turns a vector problem back into two scalar ones.
row-2-audit.cs: Equal column lengths is the invariant that makes re-zipping safe. A verb that could return columns of different lengths would have no inverse.

row-3-dimension.setup: Pulling two interleaved sequences apart so each can be handled on its own.

rungs.code:
(define-values (a b) (unzip2 '((1 2) (3 4) (5 6))))
(define-values (c d) (unzip2 '((9 8))))
(display (list a b c d))
(newline)

rungs.domain: a temperature log where each entry pairs a clock hour with a reading, and the two columns need different processing
rungs.code:
(define log '((0 12) (6 9) (12 21) (18 17) (23 13)))
(define-values (hours temps) (unzip2 log))
(define (report)
  (list 'span (list (car hours) (car (reverse hours)))
        'peak-at (list-ref hours (- (length temps) (length (member (apply max temps) temps))))
        'range (- (apply max temps) (apply min temps))
        'mean-temp (/ (apply + temps) (length temps))))
(display (report))
(newline)

rungs.domain: a differential test harness running a candidate implementation against recorded expectations
rungs.code:
(define cases '((0 1) (1 1) (2 2) (3 6) (4 24) (5 121)))
(define (factorial n) (if (= n 0) 1 (* n (factorial (- n 1)))))
(define (run impl)
  (call-with-values (lambda () (unzip2 cases))
    (lambda (inputs expected)
      (let loop ((i inputs) (e expected) (bad '()) (n 0))
        (if (null? i)
            (list 'ran n 'failed (reverse bad))
            (loop (cdr i) (cdr e)
                  (if (= (impl (car i)) (car e)) bad (cons (list (car i) 'got (impl (car i)) 'want (car e)) bad))
                  (+ n 1)))))))
(display (run factorial))
(newline)

row-3-dimension.explanation: On bare numbers it is a split and the two columns are the answer. On a temperature log the two columns get genuinely DIFFERENT treatment -- hours are read positionally for span and peak location, temperatures are reduced statistically -- and the peak hour is recovered by finding a position in one column and indexing the other, which only works because the two are aligned. In the test harness the columns are consumed at different TIMES: the inputs are fed to a function one at a time and the expectations are compared against results that did not exist when the unzip happened, so the harness reports which case diverged rather than a pass or fail. Same split; what climbs is how far apart in the program the two halves travel.
row-3-dimension.meta: Rung two locates a value in one column and indexes the other by that position. That cross-column addressing is the reason the columns must come out in row order, and it is what would break if the verb sorted or deduplicated anything.
row-3-dimension.eng: A log with a time column and a value column wants both, treated differently. Splitting once and holding both names beats re-deriving either one.
row-3-dimension.math: The range and the mean summarise one column; the position of the extremum belongs to the other. Statistics and indexing are different operations on the same table.
row-3-dimension.cs: A test harness that reports which input diverged is worth far more than one that reports a count. Keeping the inputs alongside the expectations is what makes that report possible.

row-4-proof.eng-program:
(define (round-trips? rows)
  (call-with-values (lambda () (unzip2 rows))
    (lambda (a b) (equal? (map (lambda (x y) (list x y)) a b) rows))))
(display (map round-trips? '(((1 2) (3 4)) ((9 9)) () ((#f 0) (0 #f)) ((a b) (c d) (e f)))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.math-program:
(define (columns-align? rows)
  (call-with-values (lambda () (unzip2 rows))
    (lambda (a b) (and (= (length a) (length rows)) (= (length b) (length rows))))))
(display (map columns-align? '(() ((1 2)) ((1 2) (3 4)) ((1 2) (3 4) (5 6)) ((1 2 3) (4 5 6)))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.cs-program:
(define (agrees-with-maps? rows)
  (call-with-values (lambda () (unzip2 rows))
    (lambda (a b) (and (equal? a (map car rows)) (equal? b (map cadr rows)) (equal? a (unzip1 rows))))))
(display (map agrees-with-maps? '(((1 2)) ((1 2) (3 4)) () ((x y) (z w)) ((1 2 9) (3 4 8)))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.claim: Unzipping a table of two-field rows and re-zipping the columns returns the table unchanged; both columns always have exactly as many elements as the table has rows; and the two columns are precisely (map car rows) and (map cadr rows), with the first agreeing with unzip1.
row-4-proof.invariant: For all lists of rows r each of length >= 2: map(list, unzip2(r)) = r when rows have exactly two fields; |col1| = |col2| = |r|; and col1 = map(car, r) = unzip1(r) and col2 = map(cadr, r)
row-4-proof.meta: Three claims: the round trip, the length law, and agreement with the hand-written projections. What would falsify them: a re-zip that reordered or dropped a row, columns of unequal length, or a column that disagreed with map cadr on a row whose second field is #f. The ((#f 0) (0 #f)) case in the first program is exactly that -- an implementation using a falsy sentinel would lose those entries. The three-field rows appear in the second and third programs because the length law must survive truncation.
row-4-proof.eng: The round trip is what makes unzip2 safe in a pipeline that unzips, transforms one column, and re-zips. Without it the transformation would have to carry the rows along.
row-4-proof.math: zip and unzip2 form an isomorphism between pairs of equal-length lists and lists of two-element lists. That is why either direction loses nothing.
row-4-proof.cs: Agreement with map car and map cadr is the specification restated as a test. It also pins the relationship to unzip1, which is the same projection under a different name.

row-5-emergence.eng-composition:
(define (split-table rows)
  (call-with-values (lambda () (unzip2 rows)) (lambda (a b) (cons a b))))
(define (transform-column which f rows)
  (let ((c (split-table rows)))
    (if (eq? which 'left)
        (map (lambda (x y) (list (f x) y)) (car c) (cdr c))
        (map (lambda (x y) (list x (f y))) (car c) (cdr c)))))
(display (list 'left (transform-column 'left (lambda (n) (* 10 n)) '((1 a) (2 b)))
               'right (transform-column 'right (lambda (s) (list s s)) '((1 a) (2 b)))))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.math-composition:
(define (axes points)
  (call-with-values (lambda () (unzip2 points)) (lambda (xs ys) (cons xs ys))))
(define (bounding-box points)
  (let ((a (axes points)))
    (list (list (apply min (car a)) (apply min (cdr a)))
          (list (apply max (car a)) (apply max (cdr a))))))
(define (area points)
  (let* ((b (bounding-box points))
         (w (- (caadr b) (caar b)))
         (h (- (cadr (cadr b)) (cadr (car b)))))
    (* w h)))
(display (list 'box (bounding-box '((1 1) (4 7) (3 2)))
               'areas (map area '(((0 0) (2 3)) ((5 5) (5 9)) ((0 0) (4 0) (4 4) (0 4))))))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.cs-composition:
(define (case-columns cases)
  (call-with-values (lambda () (unzip2 cases)) (lambda (i e) (cons i e))))
(define (verify impl cases)
  (let* ((c (case-columns cases))
         (got (map impl (car c))))
    (let loop ((g got) (e (cdr c)) (i (car c)) (bad '()))
      (if (null? g)
          (if (null? bad) (list 'pass (length got)) (list 'fail (reverse bad)))
          (loop (cdr g) (cdr e) (cdr i)
                (if (equal? (car g) (car e)) bad (cons (list 'on (car i) 'got (car g)) bad)))))))
(define (double n) (* 2 n))
(define (off-by-one n) (if (= n 3) 7 (* 2 n)))
(display (list 'good (verify double '((1 2) (2 4) (3 6)))
               'bad (verify off-by-one '((1 2) (2 4) (3 6) (4 8)))))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.base: unzip2 separates a table of two-field rows into two aligned columns.
row-5-emergence.emergent: eng: split-table is one call; transform-column applies a function to one column and re-zips, so a table transformation becomes a column transformation and the untouched column is carried through automatically. math: axes is one call; bounding-box reduces each axis independently to a min and a max, and area is then arithmetic on those four numbers -- a geometric summary that never touches a point after the split. cs: case-columns is one call; verify maps the implementation over the input column, walks three lists in step, and reports the specific inputs where results and expectations diverged, which is a complete test runner in ten lines.
row-5-emergence.meta: Each composition splits once and then treats the two columns as independent sequences for the rest of the computation -- the eng one re-zips at the end, the math one never does, and the cs one grows a THIRD aligned list of results and walks all three together. That last move only works because the columns came out in row order and the same length, which is the pair of properties row 4 establishes.
row-5-emergence.eng: Transforming one column of a table without disturbing the other is the most common table operation there is, and doing it by splitting is cheaper to read than destructuring every row.
row-5-emergence.math: A bounding box is four independent extrema over two independent axes. Separating the axes turns a 2D problem into two 1D ones, which is the whole technique.
row-5-emergence.cs: A test runner needs inputs, expectations, and results aligned. Two of those come from one unzip and the third comes from a map, and all three stay in step because none of the operations reorder.
